narrative:
The model estimated an 84% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain, but it was high enough that the admission decision treated you as a substantial bar-risk applicant.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: a decile of 2, compared with an average of about 5.8 among accepted students. That much lower standing pushed the prediction toward bar failure. Your first-year standing was the second strongest factor: also decile 2, versus an accepted average of about 6.0, again pushing toward failure. These two signals suggested that your academic performance was consistently below the admitted group. Your LSAT score was the third most influential factor, and it helped you: 40 is above the accepted average of about 37.2, so it pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the academic-standing concerns.

Next, request feedback from the admissions office, speak with an advisor about strengthening your academic record, and consider applying later with evidence of improved performance. Retake the LSAT only if practice results show a meaningful gain, since it already helped your profile.
